paper_title: Decision-Native Multimodal Clinical Modeling via Anatomical Grounding and Confidence Calibration

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Structured clinical decisions from volumetric computed tomography (CT) require anatomically grounded predictions and calibrated confidence estimates. However, existing 3D medical multimodal models often suffer from uncalibrated autoregressive decoding and shortcut reliance on irrelevant anatomical regions. We introduce Radev, a decision-native multimodal model that integrates anatomy-guided visual compression, direct candidate prediction, and counterfactual confidence supervision. To bridge global context with fine-grained slice details, a frozen 3D encoder extracts reusable organ-level features, which are dynamically selected by the query to attend to 2D slice features within predicted anatomical bounds. The resulting compact visual tokens enable the language backbone to estimate candidate probabilities in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding. We further propose Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT) to compare predictions under intact and intervened organ representations. CCT encourages confidence to decrease when removing target-organ evidence degrades decision quality, while penalizing excessive confidence drops under unrelated-organ removal. To facilitate rigorous evaluation, we construct CT-Verdict, a comprehensive benchmark spanning binary finding presence, multiple-choice questions, and ordinal severity assessment across both in-distribution and external cohorts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Radev significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both decision accuracy and confidence calibration, while generalizing robustly under distribution shifts. Project page at https://juntaojianggavin.github.io/projects/Radev/ .

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Medical vision language models (VLMs) integrate visual inputs with natural-language queries to support diverse clinical tasks (Jiang et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026b; Yuan et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). In volumetric computed tomography (CT), clinical queries routinely target specific organs or findings to assess their presence, anatomical location, attributes, or severity. Because these judgments carry high clinical stakes, where missed findings delay intervention and false positives trigger unnecessary procedures, clinicians require reliable uncertainty estimates to flag ambiguous cases for human review (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023). However, overconfident errors undermine this safety net by making erroneous predictions appear trustworthy. Achieving safe clinical deployment therefore demands not only high diagnostic accuracy, but also rigorous confidence calibration, ensuring that models reported confidence faithfully reflects its empirical accuracy. Existing volumetric CT VLMs predominantly follow generative paradigm as shown in Fig. 1, employing 3D or hybrid encoders to autoregressively generate free-text answers or radiology reports (Wu et al., 2025; Xin et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b; Yuan et al., 2026). While these models can be adapted to closed-set clinical decisions via text generation or candidate likelihood scoring, this formulation faces three fundamental limitations. First, autoregressive decoding incurs unnecessary computational overhead for structured decisions and often yields poorly calibrated token-level probabilities. Second, detecting localized findings requires fine-grained 2D slice Figure 1 Generative VLMs vs. Decision-Native VLMs. Conventional generative VLMs are designed for open-ended reasoning and report generation, yet often rely on ungrounded visual context and yield uncalibrated confidence. Radev is decision-native model tailored for structured, organ-grounded, and confidence-aware clinical judgment. details situated within 3D organ context, where the relevant anatomical evidence shifts dynamically with the query. Third, standard answer-level supervision rewards agreement with ground-truth labels without verifying whether the prediction, or its confidence, is genuinely grounded in the target anatomy rather than spurious background correlations. Building on recent advances in decision modeling (Typesafe.ai, 2025; Tang and Chen, 2026; Tommasino and Rinaldi, 2026), we reformulate structured CT interpretation as decision process as in Fig. 1 centered on direct candidate probability estimation, query-driven anatomical evidence selection, and counterfactual confidence supervision. To this end, we introduce Radev, decision-native multimodal model that unifies anatomically grounded visual compression with counterfactual confidence calibration. Specifically, Radev utilizes frozen 3D encoder to extract reusable organ-level features, which are projected into persistent organ ledger. Given clinical query, text-guided routing mechanism selects the target organs, whose tokens attend to high-resolution 2D slice features within predicted 3D anatomical bounds. The resulting compact visual token sequence preserves global organ context while injecting localized slice evidence specifically for the queried anatomy. Paired with the question and candidate options, these tokens allow the language backbone to estimate candidate probabilities in single forward pass without autoregressive decoding. Following multimodal alignment and verdict fine-tuning across binary, multiple-choice, and ordinal tasks, we introduce Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT). By contrasting model predictions under intact, target-ablated, and control-ablated organ representations, CCT explicitly forces confidence to drop when removing target-organ evidence impairs decision quality, while penalizing unwarranted sensitivity to the removal of unrelated organs. To enable rigorous evaluation, we construct CT-Verdict, comprehensive benchmark for structured CT interpretation spanning binary finding presence, multiple-choice location and attribute queries, and ordinal severity assessment. Featuring both in-distribution (IID) and external test cohorts, CT-Verdict establishes standardized testbed for evaluating accuracy and calibration across task types and distribution shifts. Extensive experiments show that Radev-2B achieves state-of-the-art overall accuracy of 83.75% on CTVerdict-IID while substantially improving confidence calibration and out-of-distribution generalization. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: Decision-Native Architecture: We propose Radev, structured CT interpretation model that bridges reusable 3D organ ledgers with query-selected 2D slice evidence, enabling single-pass candidate probability estimation without autoregressive decoding. Counterfactual Confidence Supervision: We design Counterfactual-Calibrated Training, an interventionbased training objective that aligns predictive confidence with causal anatomical evidence by contrasting intact, target-ablated, and control-ablated organ states. Benchmark and Empirical Validation: We release CT-Verdict, multi-task volumetric CT benchmark with internal and external cohorts, and demonstrate that Radev consistently outperforms existing generative VLMs in diagnostic accuracy, confidence calibration, and robustness to distribution shifts.

sections.title: 2.1 Decision Model
sections.content: Direct prediction over candidate answers has been explored in language and vision language modeling. BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) scores candidate continuations for multiple-choice inference, while LXMERT (Tan and Bansal, 2019) predicts answers from predefined vocabulary conditioned on an image and question. These discriminative formulations provide an established basis for making decisions without free-text generation. Recent decision-native language models revisit this principle through interfaces that accept task description and an explicit candidate set and return candidate probabilities. Jev (Typesafe.ai, 2025) is one such system, mapping typed state and discrete candidates to decision distribution in single forward pass. Open replicas fine-tune general-purpose backbones with decision heads or pointer readouts like Kev (Palmer, 2026), decider (Marosi, 2026), OneJev (OmniJev Team, 2026), ReJev (Joe-rq, 2026), which retain the autoregressive backbone but score candidates. The decision interface has recently been extended to vision and other modalities. Intern-Decision (Zhu et al., 2026) couples Qwen3.5 backbones to return an answer distribution over text states with optional images in one forward pass. OmniJev (Xu et al., 2026a) and Clef (Cloudflare, 2026) accept text, image, audio, and video. OmniMed-Jev (Tang and Chen, 2026) couples visionlanguage backbone with decision-native calibration to answer questions across different medical modalities. PathJev (Tommasino and Rinaldi, 2026) trains decision head on histopathology patches and shows that candidate scoring with dedicated head outperforms reading probabilities off generative models language head. However, all of them ingest 2D images and none consumes 3D volumetric studies, which are ubiquitous and indispensable in clinical medical imaging.

sections.title: 2.2 Medical Vision Language Model
sections.content: VLMs are now widely used in medical imaging, answering report generation and visual question-answering. The domain-specific nature of medical images has given medical VLMs distinct set of design choices. One family retains standard 2D architectures. LLaVA-Med (Li et al., 2023) establishes this paradigm via concept alignment and instruction tuning. HealthGPT (Lin et al., 2025) introduces H-LoRA plugins to unify medical comprehension and generation. Despite these advances, their visual inductive bias remains 2D without volumetric supervision. Consequently, volumetric images like CT studies are reduced to 2D slices, compromise formalized by Hulu-Med (Jiang et al., 2025), which processes slices as patch sequence via rotary-position-adaptive encoding. To reduce inter-slice redundancy, CARVE (Yi et al., 2026) frames training-free token compression as budget-constrained 2.5D allocation problem to retain salient visual evidence. second family integrates 3D encoders, addressing two key bottlenecks: volumetric token explosion and the lack of web-scale 3D corpora. To tame token complexity, RadFM (Wu et al., 2025) relies on interleaved 2D/3D generative pretraining, M3D-LaMed (Bai et al., 2024) enforces fixed token budget via spatial-pooling perceiver, and Med3DVLM (Xin et al., 2025) substitutes dense 3D attention with efficient decomposed convolutions. To compensate for data scarcity via rich supervision, CT-CHAT (Hamamci et al., 2026) reuses frozen CT-CLIP encoder, while Merlin (Blankemeier et al., 2024) pretrains 3D ResNet jointly on reports and EHR codes. Bridging both worlds, hybrid models retain 2D priors while injecting 3D cues modularly: OmniCT (Lin et al., 2026b) and TIF-GRPO (Lin et al., 2026a) combine 3D positional encodings with mask-guided organ token aggregation, and ClinFusion (Yuan et al., 2026) fuses 3D volumes with 2D foundation features via local cross-attention. Despite these advances, decision VLMs tailored for 3D medical imaging remain largely unexplored. Figure 2 Framework of the proposed Radev. (a) The Organ-Grounded Visual Encoder uses organ masks and learned mask queries to extract 3D organ tokens. Question-selected organ tokens attend to 2D slice features within their anatomical bounds. The language backbone and candidate scoring head predict an answer distribution in single forward pass. (b) Training proceeds through projectorevidence alignment, verdict fine-tuning, and Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT). (c) CCT constructs factual, target-ablated, control-ablated, and evidence-blind views by intervening on visual features. The first three views receive task supervision, while the evidence-blind view receives confidence-margin penalty.

sections.title:
3.1 Task Definition and Overview
Given a 3D CT volume V and a clinical question q with candidate answers C(q), Radev predicts a distribution
pθ(c | V, q) over the candidates. We consider binary finding presence, multiple-choice questions about finding
location or attributes, and ordinal severity assessment. Each question has exactly one reference answer.
sections.content: Radev combines an Organ-Grounded Visual Encoder with Qwen3.5 language backbone and candidate scoring head  (Fig. 2)  . The encoder uses organ masks to guide 3D organ-token readout and region-restricted attention to incorporate question-relevant 2D slice evidence. Projector-evidence alignment and verdict finetuning (VFT) directly supervise candidate probabilities. Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT) then combines task supervision across intact and ablated representations with confidence constraint on an evidence-blind view.

sections.title: 3.4 Counterfactual-Calibrated Training
sections.content: Supervision on intact inputs does not directly constrain confidence when anatomical evidence is withheld. Initialized from the VFT checkpoint, Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT) combines supervision across different evidence conditions with an explicit confidence constraint on an evidence-blind view. (4) (5) Counterfactual views. CCT replaces the 3D features of selected slots with the shared missing-feature placeholder before the MLP in Eq. (2) and disables their 2D evidence updates. Each affected evidence token then reduces to its intervened ledger token, ek = hk, preserving the interleaved token layout. For volume and question mapped to organ set B(q), CCT evaluates four views sharing the same question text and gold answer. The factual view retains all extracted 3D features and 2D evidence updates. The target-ablated view replaces all bound organs in B(q) together with the global slot n+1, while retaining unbound organs. The evidence-blind view replaces all n+1 visual slots with placeholders and disables all 2D updates, removing every image-derived feature while preserving the placeholder token sequence. sections.title: 4 CT-Verdict Benchmark
sections.content: CT-Verdict pairs 3D CT volumes with structured clinical questions and candidate answers to evaluate decision performance on in-distribution and external data. It covers the three task types defined in Sec. 3.1.

sections.title: 4.1 Question Construction and Verification
sections.content: Radiology reports are first parsed into structured finding records containing the finding, its associated organ or anatomical region, and its polarity, with optional attributes such as severity, size, number, laterality, and relations to neighboring structures. Fixed synthesis rules convert these records into question text, candidate sets, and reference labels. Binary questions use No/Yes answers, multiple-choice questions contain two to five candidates, and ordinal questions use five severity levels from 0 to 4. Two independent LLM readers answer each question using its source sentence, and their answers are compared with the rule-derived label. Disagreements are reviewed by third reader. random sample is additionally audited by human reader. Questions that fail the reader-consistency criterion are discarded rather than relabeled. Question synthesis and label verification are separate stages, with the former determining the question text and reference labels and the latter checking their agreement with the source reports.

sections.title:
4.2 Data Sources and Splits
CT-Verdict-IID. Merlin-CT (Blankemeier et al., 2024) supplies 25,270 contrast-enhanced and non-enhanced
abdominal CT studies with paired reports for training and in-distribution evaluation. All questions from
the same study are assigned to the same split. The test set contains 56,825 questions from 5,080 studies,
comprising 37,925 binary (noul), 16,210 multiple-choice (choice), and 2,690 ordinal (score) questions
across 17 organ systems and 30 clinical findings.
sections.content: CT-Verdict-OOD. The external test set uses 421 multi-centre CT studies with reports from AMOS-MM (Ji et al., 2024). It contains 2,055 questions, comprising 1,195 binary, 801 multiple-choice, and 59 ordinal questions across 12 organ systems and 24 clinical findings.

sections.title: 4.3 Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: For binary and multiple-choice questions, we report per-question accuracy (Acc), balanced accuracy (mBAcc), and area under the ROC curve (mAUC). The latter two metrics are macro-averaged across the disease categories represented in the questions. For ordinal severity, we report mean absolute error (MAE), the normalized ranked probability score (KRPS) (Epstein, 1969), and quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) (Cohen, 1968), measuring prediction error, ordinal probabilistic accuracy, and chance-corrected ordinal agreement, respectively. We also evaluate probability calibration using top-label expected calibration error (ECE) (Guo et al., 2017) and the multiclass Brier score (Glenn et al., 1950). To disentangle miscalibration from discrimination, we further apply the Murphy decomposition and report reliability (REL) and resolution (RES) (Murphy, 1973).

sections.title:
5.1 Implementation Details
Model configuration. We instantiate the 3D branch with the frozen RADAR segmentation-and-encoding
network (Zhang et al., 2026), which is never trained on the source of CT-Verdict test set.
It provides
256-dimensional organ readouts (d = 256) for 36 organ slots and one global slot (n = 36). Each organ is
read out from the first processing window that contains it in full. The global feature uses its own query,
attention module, and projection to aggregate all multi-scale tokens from a separate unwindowed pass over a
differently preprocessed copy of the volume. Both the 2D vision encoder and the language backbone are from
Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026).
sections.content: Supervised configuration. During projectorevidence alignment, the Qwen3.5 language backbone and native 2D vision encoder are frozen while the organ projector and evidence attention are trained. VFT jointly updates the language backbone, 2D vision encoder, and bridging modules. The 3D branch remains frozen throughout training. In Eq. (6), we use λb = 0.1 and λrps = 0.5. Training. All models run on four 96-GB H20 GPUs with study-level data-parallel sharding, so all questions of one study are handled by one rank. Both supervised phases use an effective batch of 32, AdamW (Ilya et al., 2019) with fresh optimizer state at each phase. We train for 1,000 steps at 103 learning rate in alignment phase, an epoch at 2 105 in VFT phase and 700 steps at 4 106 in CCT phase. Inference. Our model is read out exactly as it is trained, through the restricted softmax of Eq. (4). For baselines, likelihood readout softmaxes the summed token log-probabilities of teacher-forced candidate strings under each models chat template to obtain the answer and full candidate distribution. Decision models expose no generation path, whereas GPT-5.4 returns text without candidate log-probabilities. Slice counts follow each baselines official 3D configuration where available; otherwise, they default to 32, or are capped at the models maximum input limit if it only supports few images.

sections.title:
5.3 Confidence Analysis
How reliable are the confidence estimates? A model can predict the correct answer while assigning an inaccurate
confidence score. We therefore evaluate whether its confidence agrees with how often its predictions are correct.
Figure 3 summarizes two aspects of confidence quality. Reliability error (REL) measures the gap between
average confidence and accuracy within confidence groups, with lower values indicating better calibration.
Resolution (RES) measures how much accuracy differs across these groups. Together, these terms assess
whether assigning different confidence scores to individual predictions improves on simply reporting the
model’s overall accuracy for every prediction. Under this evaluation, 14 of the 22 baselines perform worse
than this constant-confidence reference, whereas Radev achieves a positive Brier skill score of 0.193 and a
top-label ECE of 0.010. This reduces calibration error by one to two orders of magnitude over the strongest
baselines, demonstrating that Radev uniquely combines state-of-the-art diagnostic accuracy with directly
trustworthy confidence estimates.
sections.content: Selective prediction via confidence-based rejection. Figure 4 demonstrates how confidence-based rejection turns Radevs reported probabilities into an actionable clinical safety control. Deferring the least confident Figure 4 Accuracy under confidence-based rejection. Samples are rejected in ascending order of predictive confidence. The rejection rate is the percentage of all samples rejected, and accuracy is computed over the retained samples. 20%, 40%, and 50% of cases to human readers steadily raises Radev-2Bs retained accuracy from 83.8% to 90.0%, 95.2%, and 97.0%. In contrast, no baseline matches this reliability at any deferral rate up to 90%: the strongest baseline (Jev-1.14) attains only 77.6% accuracy at 50% deferral. 5.4 Ablation Studies
Vision encoder architecture. Table 4 ablates the organ-grounded visual encoder on CT-Verdict-IID after VFT.
Pure 2D slice encoders struggle to capture volumetric continuity. Conversely, a pure 3D encoder substantially
boosts volumetric discrimination, and naive 2D–3D token concatenation yields only marginal gains. Replacing
naive fusion with our design achieves the best overall performance across all tasks. Component-wise ablations
confirm the role of each design in our organ-ledger representation: removing 3D spatial box grounding,
learned organ identity embeddings, or the global context slot consistently hurts diagnostic discrimination.
Finally, scaling the 2D stream to 32 slices under our design yields monotonic gains in mAUC across both
noul and choice, demonstrating that organ-gated cross-attention effectively harvests fine-grained slice
cues without suffering from token dilution. To isolate architectural gains from training data effects, Table 5
compares Radev-2B-VFT with baselines fine-tuned under the identical VFT configuration on CT-Verdict.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Radev, decision-native multimodal framework for structured 3D abdominal CT interpretation, alongside the CT-Verdict benchmark. By coupling reusable 3D organ ledger with question-bound 2D slice evidence, Radev predicts closed-set answer distributions in single forward pass without autoregressive decoding, while CCT anchors confidence in anatomical evidence by contrasting intact, ablated, and evidenceblind views. Across both CT-Verdict-IID and external CT-Verdict-OOD evaluations, Radev achieves state-ofthe-art diagnostic accuracy and calibration skill, delivering directly trustworthy probabilities for selective prediction and clinical abstention. In future work, we will extend the organ-grounded ledger and counterfactual calibration framework to other volumetric imaging modalities, particularly multi-sequence MRI, as well as broader anatomical regions.

Section B.2: Population-Level Analysis of Counterfactual Confidence Tempering (Proposition 1 & Proof) Section B.3: 2D-3D Feature Fusion in Vision Encoder (Spatial Membership Rule) Additional CT-Verdict Details Figure A1 Overview of CT-Verdict. (a) Benchmark construction process: radiology reports are parsed into structured findings; synthesis rules over presence, attributes, and relations turn each finding into candidate questions; questions are generated deterministically and their labels verified by three LLM readers with human spot-checking; finally, study-level split separates training from test. (b) Examples of the three question types: binary presence (noul), multi-way choice, and ordinal severity (score). (c) Details of dataset: distributions of question types and clinical tasks, dataset splits, and organ/disease coverage. This section summarizes the more details that supplement the benchmark description in the main text. Overview of the benchmark can be seen in Figure A1. A.1 Dataset Statistics Anatomical coverage. CT-Verdict spans 17 anatomical organ and region categories, with detailed persplit statistics provided in Table A1. The training (223,286 questions) and CT-Verdict-IID test (56,825 questions) splits exhibit nearly identical anatomical distributions, led by the liver/biliary tree, lower thorax, kidneys/ureters, gastrointestinal tract, and gallbladder. In contrast, the external CT-Verdict-OOD test split focuses on core abdominal anatomy (led by kidneys/ureters, peritoneal cavity, and liver/biliary tree) while omitting lower-thorax, systemic/triage, abdominal-wall, bladder, and uterus categories. Clinical tasks and disease distribution. Tables A2 and A3 report the distributions across the five major clinical capabilities (plus residual Other category of fine-grained attribute questions) and the 30 annotated diseases/findings for the training, IID test, and OOD test splits. The training and IID test splits match closely across both task capabilities and individual findings, following natural long-tailed clinical distribution. Conversely, CT-Verdict-OOD concentrates on disease discrimination and organ abnormality identification (without acute triage or laterality items), omits six thoracic-adjacent or cardiovascular findings, and re-weights toward targeted abdominal pathologies such as lymphadenopathy, ascites, splenomegaly, and renal cysts. To ensure high label fidelity, candidate questions generated by our rule-based pipeline undergo strict multi-reader verification gate before release. As shown in Table A4, the two base LLM readers achieve strong consensus on audited report units, with an inter-reader agreement of 97.8% on CT-Verdict-IID and 96.7% on CT-Verdict-OOD. Items receiving split votes from the base readers are routed to third adjudicating reader, and any item failing to reach two-of-three majority is discarded rather than relabeled. Following verification, release-level filtering removes template-only statements and balances option distributions, yielding the final released corpus of 280,111 questions for CT-Verdict-IID (223,286 training/validation and 56,825 test). Human audit and split integrity. To validate the final released labels, we manually audited random samples of 400 items from CT-Verdict-IID and 200 items from CT-Verdict-OOD against their source radiology reports. In the IID sample, all 400 items were verified as clinically acceptable with zero factual contradictions against the source text. In the OOD sample, following secondary curation pass, all 200 sampled items were likewise confirmed to be factually aligned with the source reports, achieving 100% audit accuracy across both released benchmarks. On binary presence and multiple-choice questions, probability-based mAUC plunges by 22.67 and 22.63 points (from 87.79% to 65.12% and from 81.91% to 59.28%, respectively), while balanced accuracy (mBAcc) drops from 71.79% to near-chance (53.32%). A.3 Details for Evaluation Protocol Classification Metrics (Binary & Multiple-Choice). We report per-question exact-match accuracy (Acc), macroaveraged balanced accuracy (mBAcc), and macro-averaged area under the ROC curve (mAUC). Both mBAcc and mAUC are first computed one-vs-rest within each disease categorys questions: mBAcc as the mean of sensitivity and specificity, and mAUC using the predicted probability (the Yes probability for binary, and the option probability for multiple-choice) against the one-vs-rest gold label. These scores are then macro-averaged across categories, specifically 30 clinical findings for binary and 26 option diseases for multiple-choice, to weight rare and common findings equally. The overall mBAcc averages the two branches per finding before macro-averaging. In contrast, mAUC is reported separately per branch because the two probability scales are incommensurate. sections.title: B Additional Method Details
sections.content: B.1 Organ-Stratified Curriculum of CCT Because multi-view calibration acts directly on ablated slots, uniform sampling would under-calibrate rare anatomy. We therefore sample each of the 17 organ groups in CT-Verdict of size ng with probability interpolating between instanceand organ-uniform distributions. Group quotas are floored at 0.5% of the budget, capped at eight passes per group, and interleaved at the study-run level so that even short CCT budget (Sec. 5.1) maintains balanced calibration across all organs. πg τ , τ = 0.5, (A6) B.2 Analysis of Counterfactual Confidence Tempering We provide population-level analysis motivating how supervising counterfactual organ views under Eq. (6) and Eq. (7) couples predictive confidence to anatomical evidence rather than shortcut cues; in practice, the magnitude of this effect depends on finite-sample optimization and model smoothness, and the zero-information condition for control ablation is an idealization that holds only approximately, since unbound organs may carry residual information about the verdict. Proposition 1 (Posterior tempering under target ablation). Let Y(q) denote the reference verdict for question q. For control ablation, if I(Y ; Ec Ec, q) = 0, then (Y ˆE, q) = (Y E, q). Proof. We proceed in three steps. Step 1: Proper scoring rules. For each fixed view V, cross-entropy, the multiclass Brier score, and the ranked probability score are strictly proper scoring rules whose conditional risk EY V,q[ℓ(p, )] is uniquely minimized at p( V, q) = (Y = V, q). Strict positivity of conditional mutual information yields strict entropy increase, and strictly positive entropy over finite label set implies that the conditional distribution is not one-hot, ensuring maxm (Y = E, q) < 1. Interpretation. Under smoothness of the readout, joint supervision on factual and target-ablated views couples factual confidence to the tempered ablated posterior: when the factual target representation is close to the missing-organ baseline, factual confidence is discouraged from greatly exceeding the confidence supported by the non-target context  (Table 7)  . Because sg[] stops the gradient through c, this term directly lowers blind confidence relative to the current factual confidence and, through shared parameters, indirectly discourages evidence-independent, query-only confidence on factual inputs. B.3 2D-3D Feature Fusion in Vision Encoder The 2D and 3D channels share organ identity through deterministic 3D spatial membership rule rather than learned alignment. The hit set Sk = {iei,r,c : Mk(i, r, c) = 1} forms the exact key and value set of Eq. (3). Specifically, the geometry determines which slice tokens represent organ k, while the residual cross-attention with query hk determines their weights. When Sk is empty (e.g., if the sampled slices miss the z-range, the box lies outside the plane, or the organ is absent), the evidence token falls back to hk itself, adding zero information rather than fabricating region. Mean-pooling over the same mask yields the parameter-free, organ-level 2D summary consumed by the organ-residual variant. Both consumers share this single coordinate convention.

sections.title: C Additional Experimental Results
sections.content: C.1 Qualitative Case Study Figure A2 illustrates model behavior across both correct and incorrect predictions. On correct cases, Radev-2B consistently outputs decisive confidence (0.994 for an IID study without gallstones in (a); 0.993 for an external AMOS study with renal cysts in (b)), demonstrating that organ-grounded evidence supports reliable verdicts under both in-distribution and distribution-shifted settings. In contrast, baselines either hallucinate positive findings or remain uninformative near chance (e.g., Jev-1.14 at 0.540). Crucially, on shared failure case Figure A2 Qualitative verdicts on CT-Verdict-IID and CT-Verdict-OOD. Each row shows one axial slice, the full dataset question with its gold label, and the verdicts of GPT-5.4 (free-text), Jev-1.14 (likelihood head), and Radev-2B (ours). Rows (a) and (b) are successes of Radev on IID and OOD respectively; row (c) is failure shared by all three models, on which Radev reports the lowest confidence. where all three models miss positive renal cyst (c), only Radev-2Bs confidence collapses to 0.062, effectively flagging its own error as unreliable. Meanwhile, GPT-5.4 provides no usable score and Jev-1.14 remains uninformative at 0.540, rendering neither error interceptable downstream. This demonstrates that Radev-2B not only errs less overall, but fails loudly: simple confidence threshold would abstain on the erroneous case (c) while retaining the correct decisions in (a) and (b), converting silent failures into rejectable ones via selective prediction.
